title: Jerky Motion of Active Granular Particles
authors: Alexander P. Antonov, Marco Musacchio, Hartmut Löwen, Lorenzo Caprini
abstract: Abrupt transitions between rest and motion can render the standard Newtonian description -- based on position, velocity, and acceleration -- incomplete, requiring higher-order derivatives such as the jerk, the third time derivative of position. Here, we show that the interplay between activity and dry friction gives rise to robust jerk-dominated dynamics in self-propelled particles: the particle speed increases quadratically with time under an active force, in contrast to the linear growth expected for conventional Newtonian dynamics. We demonstrate this behavior analytically, numerically, and experimentally using active vibrobots self-propelling on a vertically vibrating plate at low vibration amplitudes, where surface asperities generate dry friction and, thus, give rise to jerky motion when combined with activity. Our results establish dry friction as a simple mechanism for realizing higher-order dynamics in active matter and suggest that jerky dynamics may arise broadly in nonequilibrium systems with frictional contacts.
summary: This work investigates jerky motion in active granular particles caused by the combination of self-propulsion and dry friction. The authors demonstrate that this interaction forces the dynamics into a jerk-dominated regime, predicting a quadratic increase in speed over time. The findings are supported by theoretical modeling, numerical analysis, and physical experiments using active vibrobots.
main_problem: The standard Newtonian description is insufficient for systems exhibiting abrupt transitions between rest and motion, necessitating the inclusion of higher-order derivatives like jerk.
main_result: The interplay between activity and dry friction robustly generates jerk-dominated dynamics, leading to quadratic speed increase ($v \sim t^2$) rather than the linear growth expected classically.
method: The study combines analytical derivations (using path integrals and Onsager-Machlup functionals) with numerical simulations and physical experiments using active vibrobots.
model_or_system: The system involves self-propelled particles (active granular particles) subjected to an active force and dry friction, which introduces a threshold for motion.
key_observables: Particle speed scaling exponent ($\alpha$), displacement scaling ($\delta r \sim t^3$), and the probability of activation.
important_parameters: Dry friction threshold force ($\Delta F$), activity strength, vibration amplitude (low vs. high), and persistence time ($	au$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on approximations such as neglecting white noise or assuming the velocity after activation is independent of the activation point.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the mechanism of jerky motion due to dry friction, compare speed evolution in jerky vs. Newtonian regimes, and show data collapse confirming cubic scaling of displacement.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical need for higher-order dynamics, models the system using active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes coupled with dry friction, derives scaling laws, and validates these predictions through both numerical simulations and physical experiments.
why_interesting: The emergence of higher-order, non-Markovian dynamics from simple frictional contacts is a general mechanism in non-equilibrium statistical physics, relevant for understanding energy dissipation and transport in complex active matter systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (a) Illustration of an active particle subject to dry friction, giving rise to jerky motion. (b) Experimental setup consisting of active vibrobots on a vertically vibrating plate. (c,d) Schematic illustration of the frictional contact. Under weak plate vibrations, the vibrobot remains strongly pinned at surface asperities, preventing active motion until the active force exceeds the dry-friction threshold (c). In this regime, the interplay between activity and dry friction gives rise to jerky motion. Under strong vibrations, pinning is greatly reduced (d), rendering dry friction ineffective and allowing persistent active motion.
